content:
Ask a class for the angle sum of a quadrilateral and half of them pause. The answer is 360 degrees, every single time, whether the shape is a tidy square or a lopsided kite. That one fact — four angles adding to 360 — opens a real share of the items in this SAT Math Quadrilaterals practice test online. Scroll down for 15 Digital SAT-style MCQs, each with an instant score and a short solution.

The quadrilateral family, sorted

Quadrilaterals are a family, and the SAT loves the family resemblances. A square is a special rectangle, and also a special rhombus. So a property of the parent shape passes straight down to the child. Here are the ones worth memorising:

ShapeSidesAngles and diagonals
ParallelogramOpposite sides equal and parallelOpposite angles equal; diagonals bisect
RectangleOpposite sides equalFour right angles; diagonals equal
RhombusAll four sides equalDiagonals meet at right angles
SquareAll four sides equalRight angles and equal diagonals

Parallelogram angles, the fast way

In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal, and adjacent angles are supplementary. So if one angle is 63 degrees, the angle across from it is also 63, and each neighbour is 117. That is often the entire question. And it takes seconds once the rule is second nature.

The formulas the SAT actually uses

You do not need a huge sheet here. A few formulas cover almost every quadrilateral item:

  • Rectangle perimeter: 2 times length plus 2 times width.
  • Rectangle area: length times width.
  • Square diagonal: side times √2.
  • Trapezoid area: one half times the sum of the parallel sides, times the height.

Take a trapezoid with parallel sides 5 and 6 and a height of 18. Add the parallel sides to get 11. Then halve it to get 5.5, and multiply by 18. So the area is 99. Clean and quick.

A common trap to avoid

Here is the mistake I see most. Students assume every parallelogram has equal diagonals. It does not — only rectangles and squares do. A plain parallelogram has diagonals that bisect each other, but they are not equal in length. So read the shape name carefully before you claim a property.

A quick worked example

A square has side length 10. Its diagonal is the side times √2, so the diagonal is 10√2. No Pythagoras needed, because the diagonal splits the square into two 45-45-90 triangles. That shortcut appears throughout this SAT Math Quadrilaterals practice test online.

questions.q: A square has side length 3. What is the length of its diagonal?
A trapezoid has parallel sides of length 5 and 6 and a height of 18. What is its area?
In a parallelogram, one angle measures 41°. What is the measure of the opposite angle, in degrees?
questions.explanation: Opposite angles in a parallelogram are equal, so it is also 41°.

questions.q: A rectangle is 11 long and 6 wide. What is its perimeter?
Which quadrilateral has four right angles and all sides equal?
questions.explanation: By its defining properties, the answer is "Square".

questions.q: A square has side length 10. What is the length of its diagonal?

questions.explanation: Opposite angles in a parallelogram are equal, so it is also 63°.

questions.q: A rectangle is 9 long and 10 wide. What is its perimeter?
Which quadrilateral has all four sides equal but not necessarily right angles?
questions.explanation: By its defining properties, the answer is "Rhombus".

questions.q: A square has side length 12. What is the length of its diagonal?
A trapezoid has parallel sides of length 11 and 9 and a height of 4. What is its area?

questions.explanation: Opposite angles in a parallelogram are equal, so it is also 125°.

In which quadrilateral are the diagonals always equal in length?
questions.explanation: By its defining properties, the answer is "Rectangle".
